title: CISA: SafePay ransomware hit over 600 critical infrastructure orgs
description: The SafePay ransomware group has targeted over 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since 2024. This group uses multiple initial access methods including credential exposure, brute force attacks, VPN exploitation, and phishing. SafePay employs double-extortion tactics by stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to leak stolen information if ransoms are not paid. The group disrupts recovery by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage backups. CISA and partner agencies recommend implementing multifactor authentication, restricting administrative privileges, and patching vulnerabilities in VPNs, firewalls, and edge devices to defend against these attacks.
aiSummary: SafePay ransomware has compromised more than 600 critical infrastructure organizations globally since August 2024. The group gains initial access through credential exposure, brute force password attacks, exploitation of VPN access (notably targeting Mullvad VPN IPs), and phishing. They leverage automated scripts to exploit known vulnerabilities in edge devices and internet-exposed systems. SafePay employs double-extortion by exfiltrating sensitive data prior to encrypting victims' systems and threatening public leaks. They also hinder recovery efforts by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage backups. Unlike affiliate-based ransomware groups, SafePay operates as a private group and has become one of the most active ransomware threats since 2025, filling the void left by BlackCat and LockBit. CISA and allied agencies advise securing networks with multifactor authentication, restricting administrative privileges, and timely patching of VPNs, firewalls, and other edge devices to mitigate risk.
aiImpact: SafePay ransomware has caused widespread disruption to critical infrastructure organizations across multiple continents. The group's double-extortion tactics increase the risk of sensitive data exposure in addition to system encryption. Their ability to delete shadow copies and reset backup devices complicates recovery efforts, potentially leading to prolonged operational downtime and data loss. The broad range of initial access methods and exploitation of common vulnerabilities in edge devices increases the attack surface for organizations. The large number of victims and ongoing activity indicate a significant threat to critical infrastructure security.
